vignette:
Mei was twenty-six when she was taken, though she would later say the captivity lasted only forty-three hours. She had been working late at a regional tax office in a midsized city, finishing a client's quarterly filings, when a man she had seen around the building-someone she'd smiled at in the elevator-followed her into the parking garage. He had a knife, and he forced her into the back of a van. For the next day and a half she was kept in a locked room, bound at the wrists and ankles, while he sat in a chair by the door and watched her. She did not scream. She did not try to run. She told herself that if she stayed very still and very quiet, if she did not provoke him, he would let her go. When the police found her-a neighbor had reported suspicious activity-she was curled against a concrete wall, her back pressed to it, her eyes fixed on the door.

In the months that followed, Mei returned to her job at the tax consultancy, but the building itself had become a minefield. She could not walk through the lobby without scanning every face, every shadow. The parking garage was impossible; she now parked three blocks away on a well-lit street and walked quickly, her keys pressed between her knuckles. At her desk, she arranged her chair so that her back was to the wall and she could see the entire open-plan floor. If a colleague approached from behind, even to ask a simple question, Mei would flinch so sharply that her shoulders would lock and her breath would catch. She had come to believe that the event had happened because of the way she acted-because she had smiled at the man, because she had not fought, because she had not screamed. The people responsible had faced no consequences; the man had been released on bail and had not yet been tried, and Mei saw his name in the news and felt a cold, hollow certainty that the system had failed her, that no one would be held to account. What frightened her most was the shame she carried about her body-the way she now felt marked, exposed, as though the memory of those hours was written on her skin. She could not bear to look at herself in a mirror for more than a few seconds.

The causal loop tightened slowly. Each time Mei startled at a sudden movement-a hand reaching toward her desk, a door opening behind her-she interpreted the reaction as proof that she was still weak, still responsible, still deserving of what had happened. The startle fed the self-blame; the self-blame made her hypervigilant; the hypervigilance made her startle more. She began listening for sounds that might mean someone was entering her apartment-the click of a lock, the creak of a floorboard-and she would lie awake in the dark, her back pressed to the headboard, her eyes on the door. She had stopped going out after work, stopped meeting friends for dinner, stopped returning calls. Her supervisor noticed her declining accuracy on complex returns, the way she would jump at the sound of the office printer, and suggested she take leave. Mei refused, certain that if she stopped working she would have nothing to hold onto.

She sought help only when she realized she had begun to avoid the bathroom in her own apartment-the small, windowless room where, during captivity, she had been allowed to use a bucket. The association was unbearable. She would hold her bladder for hours until the need was urgent, then rush in and out without looking at the mirror. What finally brought her to the clinic was not the fear or the shame, but the exhaustion. She was tired of being afraid in a room where no one else was. She was tired of the weight of a story that had not ended, of a body that would not forget. She hoped, she told the intake clinician, that someone could tell her how to stop feeling like she was still in that room.
